title: Sprouted Potatoes: When You Can Trim Them and When to Throw Them Out

seo.title: Are Sprouted Potatoes Safe to Eat?
seo.meta_description: A firm potato with a few small sprouts may be usable after removing sprouts, eyes and green areas. Discard heavily sprouted, green, soft or bitter potatoes.
seo.search_intent: Decide whether a sprouted potato is safe to use.

excerpt: A firm potato with a few small sprouts can often be used after generously removing sprouts, eyes and any green tissue. Heavily sprouted, green, soft, shriveled or bitter potatoes should be discarded.
content_html:
A small sprout does not automatically make an entire potato unusable. The concern is that sprouts, eyes, skin and green tissue can contain higher concentrations of glycoalkaloids, mainly α-solanine and α-chaconine.

A firm potato with no greening and only a few small sprouts can often be used after generously removing the sprouts, eyes and surrounding peel. A heavily sprouted, green, soft, shriveled or bitter potato is better discarded.

Quick guide

PotatoWhat to do
Firm, no green, a few small sproutsRemove sprouts, eyes and surrounding peel generously
Many or long sproutsDiscard
Large green areasDiscard
Soft, shriveled or decayingDiscard
Bitter taste or burning sensationStop eating

What are potato glycoalkaloids?

Potatoes naturally produce glycoalkaloids as defense compounds. At high enough doses they can cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhea.

EFSA identified acute adverse effects starting around 1 mg glycoalkaloids per kilogram of body weight in available human evidence. That corresponds to about 60 mg for a 132-pound / 60-kg person and 80 mg for a 176-pound / 80-kg person. You cannot determine the exact amount in a potato by sight.

Where levels are highest

Sprouts, eyes, skin and tissue just beneath the skin tend to contain more glycoalkaloids, especially after light exposure or stress.

Green potatoes

The green pigment is chlorophyll and is not itself toxic. Greening signals light exposure, which can occur alongside increased glycoalkaloid production. A potato with extensive greening is best discarded.

Does cooking destroy solanine?

Cooking can reduce glycoalkaloids, but the effect is variable. EFSA reports wide reductions depending on peeling and cooking conditions. That variability is why cooking is not a reliable rescue strategy for heavily green or sprouted potatoes.

How to store potatoes

Keep potatoes in a dark, cool, dry and well-ventilated place. Light encourages greening and warm storage accelerates sprouting.

Bottom line

A firm potato with a few small sprouts can often be trimmed and peeled generously. Discard potatoes that are heavily sprouted, broadly green, soft, shriveled or bitter.

Sources

Risk and processing information comes from the European Food Safety Authority.

faq.question: Can I eat a potato with small sprouts?
faq.answer: Usually, if it is firm and not green: remove sprouts, eyes and surrounding peel generously.

faq.question: When should a sprouted potato be thrown out?
faq.answer: Discard it if sprouts are extensive, green areas are large, the potato is soft or shriveled, or it tastes bitter.

faq.question: Does boiling remove solanine?
faq.answer: It can reduce glycoalkaloids, but not predictably enough to rescue a heavily green or sprouted potato.
